newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Big push set for China entry to world trade body.
newsitem.headline: Big push set for China entry to world trade body.

text.p: China and key members of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) have agreed on intensive talks this week in a bid to speed up negotiations on Beijing's admission to the body, trade officials said on Monday.

According to the officials and trade diplomats in Geneva, Chinese negotiators would take part in three days of informal, "no holds barred" sessions of the WTO working party on China's entry from Tuesday to thrash out major problems.

These sessions will be followed by a formal meeting of the body, which is open to all 130 WTO members, late on Thursday to establish what progress had been made and to agree on the date for a new round of negotiations -- probably in the late summer.

"This is perhaps the most important week so far in this negotiation," said a senior envoy from one of the major trading powers which with other WTO member countries has been involved over the past decade in talks with Beijing on the issue.

"We are still relatively far away from a deal," said another key ambassador to the WTO. "But a lot of things could happen quite quickly if there is a real push and we get the right signals from China."

Officials in several trade missions discounted suggestions that the Chinese delegation, headed by assistant foreign trade minister Long Yongtu, might be constrained by a review of policy in the wake of the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

In bilateral talks with key powers including the European Union, the United States and Japan last week, diplomats said, there had been no indication from the Beijing team of any shift to either a harder or a softer line.

"We are still plugging away at the same issues," said one. He and others voiced doubts that Deng, who died on February 19 aged 92 after three years out of public view, had exercised any real influence on trade-related economic policy for some time.

"We are basically dealing with the same leadership as before," said another senior envoy, suggesting that clear differences within the Beijing hierarchy on the benefits, or otherwise, of joining the WTO remained.

U.S. officials in Geneva made no formal comment on their contacts so far with Long's delegation in this round of the negotiations, started in 1987 but suspended for two years after the suppression of a "democracy movement" in China in 1989.

One U.S. source said there was no sign of change in areas like trading rights for foreign companies and access to the Chinese market for foreign services like banks and insurance companies. "But we're working on it," he added.

Before the talks got under way last week, Deputy U.S. Trade Representative Jeffrey Lang told a Congressional sub-sommittee in Washington he doubted whether an agreement among all 130 WTO members to admit Beijing could come in the near term.
"China maintains many trade barriers that must be eliminated and we need to ensure the necessary changes are made before accession occurs," he said.

Trade envoys from other WTO powers said they believed it was important to encourage China to move quickly to make firm pledges on adapting its long state-controlled economy to WTO rules because of political problems in the United States.

"There is a window of opportunity now open in the wake of President Clinton's re-election. But there is a lot of resistance in Congress to closer ties with China, and the window could close," said one.
